title: Here’s How the Trump Administration Is Trying to Undermine the Election
gist: Ahead of the midterms, the DOJ under Attorney General Todd Blanche and DHS have pursued voter-roll demands, lawsuits, criminal threats and noncitizen-voting claims in California, Alaska, Nevada and Washington, nearly all rejected by courts or debunked by state officials. Experts say the efforts are faltering legally but are designed to lay groundwork for disputing results if the vote goes against the president.

themes.theme: Federal pressure campaign on election administration

insights.claim: Over the past year the DOJ has demanded unredacted voter rolls, issued executive orders to take control of elections from states, raided election offices, proposed laws that would disenfranchise millions, and claimed mass noncitizen voting.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Federal-state conflict over election administration is escalating into a systemic institutional risk.

insights.claim: The DOJ sent letters to election officials in all 50 states threatening criminal action if they failed to preserve election records for 22 days.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Criminal threats against local officials raise pressure on election administration staff.
insights.locator: There have also been escalating threats

insights.claim: Experts say the DOJ's legal efforts are faltering but are designed to lay groundwork for questioning the election results.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Expect post-election legitimacy disputes regardless of litigation outcomes.
insights.locator: Experts say that while the DOJ’s

insights.claim: UCLA's Shelby Wayment argues the administration is filing cases it knows it will lose so it can later claim the election was fraudulent.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Litigation losses are a feature, not a bug, of a delegitimization strategy.
insights.quote: They're trying to file these now knowing they have virtually no chance of winning and then after they can claim the election was fraudulent.

insights.claim: David Becker predicts that if the election does not go the president's way, the administration will try to sow doubts and possibly challenge the results, though he is not worried because institutions have held firm.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
entities: Center for Election Innovation and Research
insights.so_what: Post-election challenges are near-certain but expected to fail.

insights.claim: Justin Levitt characterizes the actions as mostly marketing and a show of force, stressing that state and local officials, not the federal government, run elections.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Federal leverage over the mechanics of elections is structurally limited.
insights.quote: What you’re seeing now is a ton of marketing.

insights.claim: Becker says the DOJ is violating its own written rules against investigative activity close to an election, rules Todd Blanche himself cited when representing Donald Trump in September 2024.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Norm erosion inside DOJ is a governance risk signal.

insights.claim: A DOJ spokesperson said the department follows the facts and law, not a political timetable, and noted the previous administration's DOJ sued Alabama and Virginia ahead of the 2024 election over voter-roll removals.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: The administration frames its actions as continuity with prior DOJ practice.
insights.quote: This Department is following the facts and the law, not anyone’s political timetable,

insights.claim: According to the Brennan Center, 34 federal district courts have ruled against President Trump since he took office in 2025, blocking voter-roll access and executive orders.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Courts are acting as an effective check on federal election interventions.

insights.claim: A federal judge rejected the DOJ's request to force California to sequester mail-in ballots tied to about 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters, and an appeals court quickly denied the DOJ's appeal.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Judicial rejections are coming quickly, limiting pre-election disruption.

insights.claim: Judge David Carter wrote that never before in American history had the federal government on the eve of an election sought to coerce states to abandon their constitutional election procedures.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Judiciary explicitly frames the moves as unprecedented.

insights.claim: An analysis by the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights found over 40 percent of the DOJ's roughly 20,000 California names were not even in the state's current voter files; the DOJ responded by suggesting contempt charges for publishing the analysis.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Federal noncitizen-voter lists show severe data-quality problems.
insights.locator: Last week, a federal judge also ruled

insights.claim: Despite repeated court losses, the DOJ issued grand jury subpoenas to California local election officials, signaling it has no intention of backing down.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Escalation is continuing through the election window.

insights.claim: The DOJ sued to block certification of Alaska's US Senate race if Democrat Mary Peltola wins, citing a spoiler candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., whose name resembles incumbent Republican Daniel Sullivan, even though the Alaska Supreme Court ruled he could stay on the ballot.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Senate control could hinge on contested certification in a close race.

insights.claim: Alaska governor Michael Dunleavy ordered a state investigation into Peltola and said he could not commit to certifying her victory while it was ongoing.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: State-level certification refusal is a concrete tail risk for Senate outcome timing.

insights.claim: A federal judge threw out the DOJ's Alaska lawsuit as likely violating Alaskans' right to a secret ballot, and the DOJ appealed within hours.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Litigation will likely extend past election day.

insights.claim: Peltola's campaign denied involvement in placing the spoiler on the ballot after a New York Times investigation alleged Democrat-aligned operatives were involved; Trump said she should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Spoiler allegations give the administration a pretext for post-election challenges.

insights.claim: DHS claimed in July to have identified over 270,000 noncitizen voters in California, Nevada, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, but the claim began to unravel.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Headline federal voter-fraud numbers are unreliable.
insights.locator: In July, the Department of Homeland Security

insights.claim: DHS's claim of 15,903 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls dropped to 185 after officials conceded they lacked evidence, and Nevada said its records showed the 185 were citizens.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: The federal data-matching methodology has collapsed under scrutiny.
insights.quote: As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens,

insights.claim: DHS says it cross-referenced publicly available state voter rolls against its records of known illegal aliens, calling the process 'not rocket science'.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: Simple database matching is producing large false-positive rates.

insights.claim: Washington secretary of state Steve Hobbs rejected a DOJ demand to isolate ballots of 400 alleged noncitizens, saying the DOJ gave no individualized proof or sourcing and raised concerns too close to the election.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: States are uniformly resisting federal ballot-isolation demands.
insights.quote: If you had valid concerns about voter registrations, the time to raise them was a month ago.

insights.claim: Verified incidents of noncitizen voting are vanishingly rare according to multiple bipartisan investigations.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: The factual basis for federal interventions is weak.

insights.claim: In Texas, the Potter County Republican Party sued to block certification unless all ballots are hand-counted, citing unevidenced claims that AI can hack any voting machine undetected and the use of Chinese-made machine parts.
insights.speaker: Tess Owen
insights.so_what: AI-hacking narratives are now being weaponized in election litigation, pressuring voting-tech vendors.
